title: Irena Sendler and the Children in the Jars
text:
Irena Sendler was a social worker for the city of Warsaw when the Germans sealed hundreds of thousands of Jews inside the Warsaw Ghetto in 1940. Her job gave her a pass to enter the ghetto to check for contagious diseases. She and her colleagues used it to bring in food and medicine, and then to bring children out.

She worked with Zegota, the underground Council to Aid Jews founded in late 1942, and in 1943 became head of its children's section. Children were smuggled out through the courthouse on the ghetto edge, through sewers, in ambulances, hidden in boxes or under tram seats. They were given false Christian names and placed with Polish families, in convents and in orphanages. Sendler kept coded lists of their real names so they could one day be reunited with their families, and hid the lists in jars buried in a friend's garden.

In October 1943 the Gestapo arrested her. She was tortured, but did not betray the network, and she was sentenced to death. Zegota bribed a guard, who let her escape on the way to execution. She continued her work under a false name. Yad Vashem honored her in 1965, though she remained little known in the wider world until the 2000s.
lesson: Ordinary jobs can become instruments of great courage. Use whatever access and skills you have to protect those who cannot protect themselves.
source: Yad Vashem, Righteous Among the Nations file on Irena Sendler; Anna Mieszkowska, Irena Sendler: Mother of the Children of the Holocaust (2010)
caveat: The often cited figure of 2,500 children saved by her network is disputed by some historians, who think the real number was lower.
